list.listitem: Offer the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine to adolescents who are 11 to 14 years, or as early as 9 years of age if indicated. Vaccination is also recommended through age 45 years for those not adequately vaccinated when younger. B

Start cervical cancer screening at age 21 years (USPSTF) or 25 years (ACS). Stop screening after age 65 years in women who have been adequately screened and are not at high risk due to previous abnormal smears or a previous diagnosis of cancer. Do not screen women who are post-hysterectomy for benign disease. A For vaccinated women, cervical cancer screening should continue as recommended for the general population. B Develop systems to identify and offer screening to women in your practice who have never or rarely had cervical cancer screening. B

USPSTF guidelines recommend Pap smear screening alone, either conventional or liquid, every 3 years from ages 21 to 29 years. For women between the ages of 30 and 65 years, Pap smear every 3 years, Pap smear and HPV co-testing every 5 years, or HPV testing alone every 5 years are options. Co-testing and HPV alone every 5 years have a similar effect on cancer incidence and mortality. A
Follow-up of an abnormal screening test should follow 2019 risk based guidance from ASCCP ().A

Women aged 30 years and older who are cytology-negative but HPV-positive should either repeat dual testing in 12 months or undergo immediate HPV genotype-specific testing for HPV-16 and HPV-18. C Options for treatment of CIN are observation, excision (hysterectomy, cold-knife cone biopsy, loop electrosurgical excision procedure [LEEP]), or ablation (cryotherapy, thermal coagulation) of the cervical transformation zone. Excisional techniques reduce the risk of treatment failure, A but increase the risk of subsequent preterm birth. B

National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines (2023) provide guidance regarding treatment of disease by stage. B Conization may be considered for those who meet strict criteria including no lymphovascular space invasion. B Open radical hysterectomy results in better outcomes than minimally-invasive surgery for those with early-stage disease. B

background.definition: There are three approaches to screening for cervical cancer: the conventional Papanicolaou (Pap) smear, thin layer liquid preparations, and screening for HPV. Although no randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have demonstrated that screening for cervical cancer decreases overall mortality, the introduction of Pap smear screening has consistently been followed by a decrease in the incidence of invasive cervical cancer and cervical cancer deaths. Pathology results, whether for cytology or colposcopic biopsy, include the following: atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US); low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL); high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL); cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), further graded by severity as 1-3, and cervical cancer (Table 1). Another category resulting from co-testing is NILM which means HPV-positive but negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. The 2018 International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) uterine cervical cancer staging system includes 4 stages. Stage I is carcinoma confined to the cervix and is further divided into IA and IB based on depth of invasion (including 2 subdivisions for 1A and further subdivisions of IB based on tumor size. Stage II is carcinoma invading beyond the uterus but not extended onto the lower third of the vagina or the pelvic wall; Stage IIA is further subdivided based on tumor size. Stage III is carcinoma involving the lower third of the vagina and/or extending to the pelvic wall and/or causes hydronephrosis or nonfunctioning kidney and/or involves pelvic and/pr para-aortic lymph nodes. Stage III is further subdivided into A-C depending on extent of disease in those structures. Stage IV is carcinoma that has extended beyond the true pelvis or has involved the bladder or rectal mucosa; Stage IVA is spread to adjacent pelvic organs and Stage IVB spread to distant organs.

list.listitem: Worldwide: 466,000 new cases of cervical cancer are identified annually and approximately half this number die of the disease.
United States: Over 14 000 people are diagnosed with cervical cancer and more than 4000 die from cervical cancer each year.

Netherlands: 72-month cumulative cancer incidence was 58.5 (95% CI, 54.6-62.7) per 100,000 using conventional cytology, 66.8 (95% CI, 56.7-78.7) using ThinPrep and 44.6 (95% CI, 37.8-52.6) using SurePath. In a 14-year follow-up of a population screening program of 43,339 HPV-negative women aged 29 to 61 years in the Netherlands, the cumulative incidence rates of cervical cancer and CIN3+ were 0.09% and 0.56%, respectively among women receiving dual HPV and cytology screening; this was similar to the rates seen among women receiving cytology screening only (0.09% and 0.69%, respectively).

There is a racial and ethnic disparity in the incidence of cervical cancer, although this is narrowing: 9.5/100,000 new cases occur in Hispanics and 9.0/100,000 in blacks versus 7.1/100,000 in whites, 6.1/100,000 in Asian/Pacific Islanders and 6.3/100,000 in American Indian/Alaska Natives.

Cervical cancer risk is higher among women with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). In one study of 348 HIV-positive women followed for 40 months, cervical intra-epithelial neoplasia (CIN) developed in 47 (13.5%) for an incidence of 4.1 cases per 100 person-years of follow-up. Risk factors for CIN included age <19 years (RR 2.6; 95% CI, 1.24-5.35) and not having used antiretroviral medications outside of pregnancy (RR 2.3; 95% CI, 1.31-4.19). In a systematic review of 5882 HIV-positive women, incidence ranged from 4.9 to 21.1 cases per 100 woman-years for any cervical lesion and 0.4 to 8.8 cases per 100 woman-years for high-grade lesions. Based on a meta-analysis of 24 studies including 236,127 women living with HIV, the pooled relative risk of cervical cancer was 6.07 (95% CI 4·40-8·37).

The incidence rate for cervical cancer after CIN treatment is also increased compared to the general population based on cancer registry data (39/100,000 woman-years, 95% CI 22-69 vs. 3.3/100,000, 95% CI 2.57-4.24).
The incidence of cervical cancer in the US has decreased by more than 50% in the past 30 years, likely because of widespread cervical cancer screening tests and HPV vaccination.

In 2020 in the United States, there were approximately 296,981 women living with cervical cancer. Percentages by stage (2019) are: 44% localized, 36% spread to regional lymph nodes, 16% with distant metastases, and 4% un-staged.
In the UK ARTISTIC trial with 24,510 participants, CIN 3 or higher was found in 1.27% to 1.31% of subjects at baseline.
The direct medical cost associated with the management of HPV-related disease was estimated at $2.9 billion.
Cervical cancer is the fourth most common type of cancer in women worldwide.
Approximately 0.7% of women will be diagnosed with cervical cancer during their lifetime, based on 2015–2019 data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Globally, in 2018, cervical cancer ranked fourth for both incidence and mortality among women.
HPV infection causes 95% to 100% of all cervical cancer.
Worldwide, the most common HPV types in cervical cancer were types 16 (57%), 18 (16%), 58 (5%), 33 (5%), 45 (5%), 31 (4%), 52 (3%), and 35 (2%).

The HPV genome encodes for eight proteins that facilitate the integration of the viral genome into the host by damaging several cellular pathways in the host cells, slowly progressing to cervical cancer over time. HPV-induced cancer likely involves numerous chance events such as mutation, integration, and host genetic changes.
Only a small fraction of women infected with the HPV progress to cervical cancer, usually after more than a decade.

Vaginal microbiota dominated by non-Lactobacilli species or Lactobacillus iners were associated with higher risk of any prevalent HPV and two to three times higher risk for high-risk HPV and cervical cancer or dysplasia compared with Lactobacillus crispatus. Authors of another systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies found similar results with lactobacillus spp. associated with decreased detection of high-risk subtype (hr)HPV infection (OR 0.64; 95% CI, 0.48-0.87), CIN (OR 0.53; 95% CI, 0.34-0.83), and cervical cancer (OR 0.12; 95% CI, 0.04-0.36). Lactobacillus crispatus but not Lactobacillus iners was associated with the decreased detection of hrHPV infection and CIN.
Other environmental factors, such as impaired host immunity and carcinogens, may allow persistence of the oncogenic virus.

High parity (>2 in most studies; risk increases with increased parity)
Oral contraception for 5 or more years
Any mucosal HPV type seropositivity (invasive cervical cancer)

list.listitem: The 2018 USPSTF and ACOG guidelines recommend screening women 21 to 29 years with cytology every 3 years. For women age 30 to 65 years, options include cytology every 3 years, HPV alone every 5 years, or HPV plus cytology every 5 years (A recommendation). Co-testing with HPV and cytology can potentially detect 5.9% more cases of cervical cancer and 3.5% more cases of precancer but has a higher false-positive rate than HPV alone based on clinical trials and modeling. Modeling studies have shown that all 3 options greatly reduce cervical cancer incidence and mortality, with the greatest reduction for HPV alone or co-testing every 5 years.
For follow-up of an abnormal cervical screening test using the 2019 ASCCP risk based algorithm see and Diagnostic Testing | Colposcopy in the Diagnosis section below.

Women older than 65 years who have had previous adequate and normal screening do not benefit from further screening. Among women who did not have screening in their 50s, the incidence of cervical cancer up to age 80 years was 5.0/1000 and, for these women, continued screening decreased cervical cancer by 3.3/1000. In the 2013 and 2015 National Health Interview Surveys, 18.4% of women aged 61 to 65 years in the 2013 and 2015 National Health Interview Surveys reported no recent cervical cancer screening, so it is important to verify recent normal screening before discontinuing.

The 2020 American Cancer Society guideline update recommends that individuals aged >65 years who have no history of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or more severe disease within the past 25 years, and who have documented adequate negative prior screening in the prior 10 years, discontinue all cervical cancer screening. The 2015 American College of Physicians guideline specifies stopping screening for women older than 65 years if they have had 3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative cytology and HPV test results within 10 years, with the most recent test performed within 5 years.

American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG, 2018) recommends continued screening for women following hysterectomy for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 2 or higher with cytology alone every 3 year for 20 years after the initial posttreatment surveillance.

The sensitivity of conventional Pap smear ranges from 30% to 87% and specificity ranges from 86% to 100% when either low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL) or higher grade or CIN I or higher grade was the threshold for detection in a screening population. For detection of CIN II or higher, a more clinically relevant finding, sensitivity was higher (44%-99%) with narrower specificity (91%-98%).

The best screening collection tool for cervical cytology appears to be extended tip spatulas; the combination of an extended tip spatula and cytobrush is the best method for sampling the ecto- and endocervix. Ayre's spatula is least effective. A sleeved cytobrush is also preferable for endocervical sampling compared to traditional curettage.

Water-soluble lubricants not containing carbomers do not interfere with Pap smear adequacy. In one study using liquid-based Pap tests, there was a higher rate of insufficient specimens when a water-soluble lubricant containing carbomers was used.

Liquid-based cytology (LBC) and other new technologies are neither more sensitive in detecting cervical cancer nor more effective in reducing mortality than conventional Pap smear screening. Positive likelihood ratios for detection of HSIL or worse are similar (19.0 vs. 16.7, respectively). However, in a population-based study from the Netherlands, sensitivity for detecting cancer was different between the two different and favored Thin-prep when comparing types of liquid-based and conventional cytology.

In a study of 1096 women who tested positive for HPV but negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (4.1% of all women screened), rescreening slides led to upgrading in 13.9% to atypical squamous cells or higher, with 2.8% upgraded to low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion or higher.

listitem.strong: Screening Using HPV Alone (including urine testing)

list.listitem: The 2020 American Cancer Society guideline update recommends that primary HPV testing, where available, is the preferred screening strategy starting at age 25 years and screening every 5 years until age 65 years.

The American Society of Clinical Oncology recommends DNA testing in all resource settings. This includes options for maximal testing every 5 years at ages 25-65 years; enhanced testing at age 30-65 years every 10 years if two consecutive negative tests at 5-year intervals; limited testing at ages 30-49 years, every 10 years; or basic testing at ages 30-49 years, one to three times per lifetime accompanied by visual inspection with acetic acid.

The sensitivity of HPV testing alone for CIN II or higher ranges from 94% to 97%, and specificity from 93% to 94% (more sensitive than conventional Pap but less specific). In a follow-up of four European RCTs, women randomized to HPV-based testing were less likely to develop invasive cervical cancer than those screened with cytology alone. The number of women developing invasive cancer was small (107 out of 1 million) and there were high dropout rates in 3 of the 4 studies. In a large randomized trial of 203,788 women in Finland, sensitivity of HPV testing was similar to that of Pap testing but caused more overdiagnosis. A single HPV test, however, provides the same degree of protection over 5 years as a Pap smear does for 3 years. In a South African prevention trial of 6555 women, those randomly assigned to HPV test and treat with cryotherapy had lower 36-month cumulative detection of CIN2 or higher than the control arm (1.5% vs. 5.6%).

Based on a modeled cost-effectiveness analysis, primary HPV testing was found to be most cost-effective with 294 cases of CIN3þ detected with 2422 colposcopies at an incurred cost of $3.47 M. Cytology screening was more expensive ($4.79 M) and detected fewer cases (285 per 99,549 women) and cytology/HPV co-testing detected 14 more cases than HPV alone but required 100,277 more cytology tests and 566 more colposcopies at a cost of $5.85 M.

In a study of 10,860 women with negative cytology at baseline, specificity of a high-risk HPV E6/E7 RNA assay for CIN2 or lower was significantly greater at 96.3% than a high-risk HPV DNA assay (specificity of 94.8%). Estimated sensitivities and risks for detection were similar. Women who were negative on both screening tests had a very low risk of CIN2+ (<0.3%) at 3 years compared with CIN2+ risk in women with a positive RNA or DNA assay (6.3% and 5.1%, respectively). Similar results showing a higher specificity (<CIN2) and positive predictive value (CIN2+) of the RNA-based Aptima HPV test over the DNA test were demonstrated in a German study of 10,040 women.

In an observational study in England of primary care cervical cancer screening of 578,547 women using either high-risk (hr)HPV screening, performed for 32% of the samples, or liquid-based cytology, baseline hrHPV testing and early recall detected substantially more CIN lesions than cytology but required approximately 80% more colposcopies (adjusted odds ratio 1.77, 95% CI, 1.73-1.82). At 3-years, the 33,506 women screened with hrHPV testing had substantially less CIN grade 3 or worse than the 77, 017 women screened with liquid-based cytology (OR 0.14; 95% CI, 0.09-0.23).

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis found that urine HPV testing had a similar rate of detection of HPV compared with cervical swab (53% vs 46% p=NS). However for CIN2 or worse, urine samples were less sensitive than both clinician-collected cervical swabs (79% vs 93%) and self-collected swabs (79% vs 89%), although in both comparisons the urine tests were more specific. Urinary testing may be an option for a patient who declines both clinician-collected and self-collected cervical swabbing.

listitem.strong: Screening Using HPV Plus Conventional Cytology Together

list.listitem: This combination is an option for women over age 30 years; low-risk women who are negative for both screens should be rescreened every 5 years. The sensitivity and specificity of using HPV and Pap testing together (dual testing or cotesting) are 100% and 92.5%, respectively.

Results from a UK RCT with 14,230 women in their 30s comparing cervical cytology screening alone to screening using HPV testing concurrent with Pap smear showed no difference in the detection of CIN 3 or higher between groups (31 total cases detected).

In a longitudinal cohort study of 2462 Brazilian women, dual testing with cytology and HPV DNA testing resulted in the best optimization of sensitivity and specificity. By allowing 12 months for the detection of lesions, however, cytology alone performed nearly as well. Similar findings were demonstrated in a Chinese pooled study analysis where co-testing with LBC and HPV had the highest sensitivity and negative predictive value, permitting a safe extension of screening intervals.

In a population-based, retrospective Swedish cohort study, HPV testing alone was a reasonable approach compared to co-testing; among those with biopsy-proven CIN2+, cytology was positive in <0.02% of individuals who had negative HPV. These results, however, were not true when testing was based on clinical indications or for unknown indication; in these cases, 3.8% of individuals with CIN2+ would have been missed without cytology co-testing.

In a Swedish randomized screening trial of 12,527 women aged 32 to 38 years, the cumulative incidence of CIN2+ was the same for HPV/cytology dual screening and for cytology at 11 years. This implies the increased sensitivity of HPV screening for CIN2+ likely reflects earlier detection rather than overdiagnosis. This was confirmed in a Chinese study with two rounds of screening in which adding hrHPV testing to cytology vs. cytology alone for primary cervical cancer screening led to earlier detection of clinically significant preinvasive lesions with higher detection rates of CIN2+ (1.01% vs. 0.66%, OR 1.53, 95% CI 1.09-2.19) over the two rounds. There was reduced detection of CIN2+ lesions in the intervention group after the first round, although with a four-fold increased rate of colposcopy (10.6% vs. 2.4%).

In the ATHENA study using cytology and HPV testing with simultaneous HPV16/18 genotyping in 34,354 women, cotesting with cytology increased sensitivity but did so by increasing testing. Strategies that included integrated HPV16/18 testing resulted in more efficient referral to colposcopy and strategies using cytology for triage of HPV-positive women decreased sensitivity and limited the number of colposcopies.

In a 10-year follow-up study of 1.2 million women aged 30 years and older who were screened using co-testing every 3 years for cervical cancer at Kaiser Permanente of Northern California, 623 women were diagnosed with cervical cancer and 5369 women with CIN grade 3 or adenocarcinoma in situ. Among women with cervical cancer, 77% had a positive HPV test result compared with 59% who had abnormal cytology. Only 5.9% of women with cancer had a negative HPV test and abnormal cytology (the added detection contribution of cytology). Among women with precancers, 84% had a positive HPV test and 62% had abnormal cytology. Only 3.5% of these women had a negative HPV test and abnormal cytology.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 27 prospective studies with 185,269 subjects found the combination of cytology (ASC-US or higher grades) and high-risk HPV testing (excepting genotyping for HPV 16 or 18 [HPV16/18]) with the either-positive criterion (OR rule) was the most sensitive/least specific, whereas the same combination with the both-positive criterion (AND rule) was the most specific/least sensitive for identifying CIN ≥ 2 in healthy asymptomatic women.

There was a sharp decrease in the proportion of women screened for cervical cancer during the pandemic - 4.24% (95% CI 2.77%-5.71%) in 2020 compared to 9.79% (95% CI 6.00%-13.59%) in 2019, based on a meta-analysis of seven studies from Slovenia, Italy, Ontario (Canada), Scotland, Belgium, and the US. Outreach efforts may be needed to encourage patients to return to screening.

Invitation letters (moderate-certainty evidence), educational materials (low-certainty evidence), and lay health worker involvement (low-certainty evidence) increase uptake of cervical screening. In a study conducted in Appalachia, a faith-based home intervention increased screening rates over control subjects (17.6% vs. 11.2% respectively reported obtaining screening).

In one study, offering non-speculum clinician-taken sampling or self-sampling increased uptake in older lapsed-attendee women (20.4% (n = 80/393) versus 4.9% in the control arm). Non-speculum vs. speculum-based clinician sampling for HPV was found to have complete concordance among women with positive CIN2+ who had a speculum sample ≤91 days prior to the non-speculum sample (n = 12) and 96.6% concordant results among women with negative cytology (n = 204); 71% percent (n = 120/170) of women preferred a non-speculum sample for their next screen.
An intervention combining community cancer education with navigation services resulted in significant increases in screening rates among under-screened Korean American women.

A Danish study found that non-participation in cervical cancer screening was more common in overweight or obese women (aOR = 1.2 to 1.5), those with poor self-perceived health (aOR = 1.2) or who smoked (aOR == 1.8). Women with a history of STI, with 10 or more lifetime partners, or with 2 or more recent partners were more likely to participate.
Telephone contact with women who have not participated in cervical cancer screening for a long time also increases participation.
Among Latinas, use of a video plus home-based educational session increased attendance for screening (53.4% vs. 38.7% for video only and 34% for usual-care).

Among women with mobility impairments, a Promoting Access to Health Services 90-minute, small-group participatory workshop with 6 months of structured telephone support was successful in increasing receipt of Pap smears over the control group (61% vs. 27%, respectively).

In a Swedish study of women who were long-time non-attendees for cervical cancer screening, offering an HPV self-test was more effective than a telephone call or standard screening invitation (24.5%, 18%, and 10.6% respectively were tested).Similar improvement in screening was seen in a French study comparing HPV self-testing vs. second invitation (18.3% vs. 2%); however, low compliance to follow-up in the self-sampling group reduced the effectiveness of this approach.

In a US study, 329 low-income women who were overdue for cervical cancer screening and offered HPV self-sampling completed testing resulting in a prevalence of hrHPV of 16%; 24 (46%) presented for in-clinic cervical cancer screening.

Authors of a meta-analysis found no difference in effectiveness between opt-in strategies (i.e., women had to request a self sampling kit) compared to invitation letters (relative participation 1.22; 95% CI, 0.93-1.61). However, direct offer of self-sampling devices to women in under-screened communities resulted in high participation rates of >75%. Substantial interstudy heterogeneity was noted. Authors of another meta-analysis found that all self-sampling invitation scenarios were more effective in reaching under-screened women compared to controls who were invited for screening according to existing practice, with send-to-all strategies being more effective than opt-in strategies. Pooled participation differences (for experimental vs. control groups was 13.2% (95% CI 11.0-15.3%) for mail-to-all, 4.4% (95% CI 1.2-7.6%) for opt-in, 39.1% (95% CI 8.4-69.9%) for community mobilization & outreach, and 28.1% (95% CI 23.5-32.7%) for offer at healthcare service.

In a cost-effectiveness analysis of results from an RCT including 36,390 women aged 30-49 years, repeat HPV self-sampling led to 1633 more screened women and 107 more histologically diagnosed CIN2+ at a lower cost (€ 229,446 vs. € 782,772) compared to midwife-collected Pap smears.
In a prospective observational study, use of menstrual pad HPV sampling conducted within 2 months was highly concordant with clinician-collected sampling, with a concordance of 94% (95% CI 83-98).

In a meta-analysis of 56 accuracy studies and 25 participation trials, authors found that hrHPV assays based on polymerase chain reaction (PCR) were as sensitive on vaginal self-samples as on clinician samples for detecting CIN2+ or CIN3+ (pooled ratio 0.99, 95% CI, 0.97 to 1.02) while high-risk HPV assays based on signal amplification were less sensitive using self-samples (pooled ratio 0.85, 95% CI, 0.80 to 0.89). Specificity to exclude CIN2+ was lower with self-samples by 2% with PCR and 4% lower with signal amplification.

The CDC recommends HPV vaccination to all adolescents at age 11 to 14 years. This can be started as young as age 9 years or as old as age 45 years. The vaccine is given in 2 doses to those age 9-14 years (2016), with the second dose given 6 to 12 months after the first. For young people ages 15 to 45 years, AAFP recommends the 3-dose series at 0, 1 to 2 months, and 6 months. Since the introduction of the HPV vaccine, rates of cervical cancer have declined. Using data from 1999-2017, investigators found a decrease in cervical squamous-cell carcinoma of 7.9% per year among women aged 15–20 years, 5.5% among women aged 21–24 years, and 2.3% among women aged 25–29 years. Similarly, rates of cervical adenocarcinoma decreased 4.1% per year among women aged 15–20 years, 3.6% per year among women aged 21–24 years, and 1.6% per year among women 25–29 years.

HPV vaccine is also recommended for gay and bisexual men (or any man who has sex with men) and persons with compromised immune systems (including HIV) through age 45 years, if they were not fully vaccinated when they were younger. The vaccine efficacy was 100% (95% CI, 80.9%-100%) for prevention of HPV 16 or 18-related cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) in phase III clinical studies. The vaccine is less effective in females previously exposed to the virus.

Investigators analyzed the added value of extending the current U.S. HPV vaccination program to women aged 27 to 45 years and men aged 22 to 45 years with respect to population-level effectiveness and cost-effectiveness and found only small additional health benefits at substantially higher incremental cost-effectiveness ratios.

A quadrivalent vaccine (Gardasil) protects against four HPV types (6, 11, 16, and 18) that are responsible for 70% of cervical cancers and 90% of genital warts in both men and women. The quadrivalent vaccine is licensed for use in males and females aged 9 to 26 years. Including women with preexisting HPV infection, the absolute risk reduction is 0.3%, and the number needed to treat (NNT) is 333. Cost for the full series is about $360.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 18 studies found that females have higher antibody titers against HPV after receiving the quadrivalent HPV vaccine compared to males. It is not clear if doses and/or schedules for vaccination should be adjusted by sex.
There is also a bivalent vaccine (HPV2, Cervarix) against HPV types 16 and 18 (which cause 70% of cervical cancers) that is licensed for females aged 9 to 25 years.

Based on results of 6 trials, bivalent and quadrivalent HPV vaccines vs. placebo reduced the rate of lesions in the cervix, vulva, vagina, and anogenital region, with efficacy of 93% (95% CI, 87-96) and 62% (95% CI, 27-70), respectively. There were more symptoms in the bivalent vaccine group (35%; 95% CI, 5-73) vs. control groups.
Efficacy appears to be maintained at 4 years. In addition, there is evidence of cross-protective efficacy of the HPV-16/18 vaccine against some oncogenic non-vaccine HPV types.

In a study of 138,693 Scottish women who had cervical screening at age 20 years, rates of CIN grade 3 or worse were identified in 0.06% of the 49% who received all 3 doses of the HPV bivalent vaccine compared with 0.59% among the 46% who were unvaccinated. The NNT to prevent 1 case of CIN 3 or worse at first screening 2 to 8 years after vaccination was 189.

In a second Scottish study of 447,845 female patients born between 1988 and 1996, 239 developed invasive cervical cancer. Two hundred and 10 cancers were found among those who were unvaccinated for a cancer incidence rate of 8.4/100,000 (95% CI 7.2 - 9.6), 8 cancers were among those partially vaccinated at 14 years or higher for an incidence rate of 6.5/100,000 (2.6-13.6), 21 cancers were among those fully vaccinated at 14 years or higher for an incidence rate of 2.7/100,000 (1.7-4.2) and none were found among those fully vaccinated at ages 12-13 years.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 65 studies published between Feb 1, 2014, and Oct 11, 2018 found a significantly reduced prevalence of HPV 16/18 of 83% (RR 0.17, 95% CI, 0.11-0·25) among girls aged 13 to 19 years and 66% (RR 0.34, 95% CI, 0.23-0.49) among women aged 20 to 24 years at 5 to 8 years post-vaccination. Anogenital wart diagnoses decreased significantly by 67% (RR 0.33, 95% CI, 0.24-0.46) among girls aged 15 to 19 years, 54% (RR 0.46, 95% CI, 0.36-0.60) among women aged 20 to 24 years, and 31% (RR 0.69, 95% CI, 0.53-0.89) among women aged 25 to 29 years. At 5 to 9 years, CIN2+ significantly decreased by 51% (RR 0.49, 95% CI, 0.42-0.58) among screened girls aged 15 to 19 years and 31% (RR 0.69, 95% CI, 0.57-0.84) among women aged 20 to 24 years. Among boys aged 15 to 19 years anogenital wart diagnoses decreased significantly by 48% (RR 0.52, 95% CI, 0.37-0.75) and among men aged 20 to 24 years by 32% (RR 0.68, 95% CI, 0.47-0.98).

Based on Finnish Cancer Registry data, with a follow-up time of up to 11 years, investigators identified 17 HPV-positive invasive cancer cases (14 cervical cancers, 1 vaginal cancer, 1 vulvar cancer and 1 tongue cancer) among 16,526 non-HPV-vaccinated subjects and no cases in the 3341 HPV-vaccinated subjects. Similarly, at a median of 11.1 years of follow-up of a Costa Rica vaccine trial, 34 (1.5%) of 2233 unvaccinated women available at follow-up had a CIN2+ outcome compared with none of 1913 women in the bivalent HPV vaccination group.
A 9-valent vaccine against HPV, including the HPV types in the quadrivalent HPV vaccine, was noninferior to the quadrivalent HPV vaccine but associated with more adverse events.

In a cohort study of women aged 15 to 25 years, women without current or prior exposure to HPV 16/18 had a vaccine efficacy rate of 90.3% (96.1%; 95% CI, 87.3-92.6) against 6-month persistent infection (PI), 91.9% (84.6-96.2) against CIN1+ and 94.6% (86.3-98.4) against CIN2+. For women with prior exposure (seropositive for HPV 16/18), vaccine efficacy was 72.3% (53.0-84.5) against 6-month PI, 67.2% (10.9-89.9) against CIN1+, and 68.8% (−28.3-95.0) against CIN2+. All women tolerated the vaccine well.

A 2026 retrospective cohort found a decreased risk of oral, digestive, respiratory, bone, soft tissue, breast, thyroid, and other cancers, in addition to cervical cancers, among women who had received the HPV vaccine compared to women matched on 8 clinical categories. Younger age at vaccination was associated with a greater reduction in risk.

Do not give the vaccine to women with a previous allergic reaction to yeast or who are pregnant; notify vaccinated women that they will still require regular Pap smear screening and that the vaccine does not prevent other sexually-transmitted infections (STIs) such as HIV.
Health education including sexual negotiation skills can reduce sexual risk-taking behavior.

A vaccine containing synthetic plasmids targeting HPV-16 and HPV-18 E6 and E7 proteins was found to be significantly more effective than placebo with respect to histopathological regression of CIN2/3 lesions; 55 (48.2%) of 114 VGX-3100 recipients and 12 (30%) of 40 placebo recipients had histopathological regression to CIN1 or normal pathology 36 weeks after the first dose.

In an RCT of 312 Iranian women with histologically confirmed residual/recurrent CIN 1 or CIN 2-3, there was a greater reduction at 2 years in the number of women with CIN 2-3 in the HPV vaccine group vs. the control group (75% reduction [from 93 to 23] versus 40% reduction [from 69 to 41]).

HPV vaccination compared to surgical excision alone for women undergoing excisional treatment of CIN3 resulted in a significant risk reduction in development of recurrent high grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.27, 0.64; NNT 45.5) based on a meta-analysis of 10 studies including 21,059 patients (3,939 post vaccination and 17,150 controls). Authors of a meta-analysis including 18 studies also found a reduced risk of recurrence of CIN2+ among vaccinated compared with non-vaccinated patients (11 studies, 19,909 participants; risk ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.60; I2=58%). With only 3 studies, there was larger uncertainty (I2=71%) for studies of those with CIN3.

Authors of a literature review concluded that the commercially-available three-dose, quadrivalent HPV vaccine may be effective for treatment of cutaneous warts, recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, and squamous and basal cell carcinomas and non-commercially available HPV vaccines appear effective for treatment of anogenital warts, CIN, anal intraepithelial neoplasia, and vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia.
Retinoids (vitamin A derivatives) are not effective in preventing progression of CIN of any grade but may be associated with regression of CIN2.

Among women with abnormal cancer screening test results, use of a patient navigator decreased the time to definitive diagnostic test or evaluation by 11 days for black patients, 6 days for Hispanic patients, and 2 days for white patients.
Direct visualization of the cervix with colposcopy and colposcopy-guided biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis of cervical cancer.

For pretreatment planning of invasive cervical cancer, the American College of Radiology recommends magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pelvis without and with IV contrast and fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography-computed tomography (FDG-PET/CT) whole body as appropriate for staging. B

In patients with early-stage cervical cancer, physical examination findings can be normal; most women are asymptomatic at the time of diagnosis. As disease progresses, women may present with vaginal discharge, abnormal vaginal bleeding, dyspareunia, or postcoital bleeding; postcoital bleeding is of limited use based on a systematic review that found only 1 in 220 women with this symptom had invasive cervical cancer.
The cervix may become firm and abnormal in appearance, with gross erosion, ulcer, or mass. These abnormalities can extend to the vagina.
Cervical ectopy does not appear to be a risk factor for HPV acquisition in healthy young women.

Rectal examination can help determine cervix size and may reveal an external mass or gross blood from tumor erosion. Parametrial extension is also best determined by findings of nodularity on rectal exam.

Bimanual examination findings can reveal pelvic metastasis. Palpate the supraclavicular and groin lymph nodes to exclude metastatic disease. There are no trials examining the effectiveness of the pelvic examination in reducing all-cause mortality or cancer-specific morbidity and mortality or improving quality of life.

Leg edema suggests lymphatic/vascular obstruction from tumor and, if the disease involves the liver, some patients develop hepatomegaly. The triad of leg edema, pain, and hydronephrosis suggests advanced cervical cancer with pelvic wall involvement.
Pulmonary metastases are difficult to detect on physical examination unless pleural effusion or bronchial obstruction becomes apparent.
Bowel or urinary symptoms such as hematuria, hematochezia, or pressure-related complaints signal advanced disease.
Offer women the option of placing feet at the end of the examination table as this can be more comfortable than using stirrups.

Direct visualization of the cervix with colposcopy and colposcopy-guided biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis of cervical cancer. Consensus guidelines developed by the American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology were revised in 2019 for managing abnormal cervical cancer screening tests. The 2019 management recommendations, ranging from deferred colposcopy to expedited treatment without colposcopic biopsy, are based on risk not test results and better align with the understanding of the natural history of HPV and cervical carcinogenesis. The method for estimating risk is outlined in an additional ASCCP publication. Refer to and to their Web site for an interactive calculator to assist physicians in determining appropriate follow-up for women with cervical abnormalities. Some key recommendations are as follows: Estimated 5-year CIN 3+ risk of <0.15% based on past history and current test results (e.g., negative HPV test and co-test), perform routine screening at 5-year intervals using HPV-based testing. Estimated 5-year CIN 3+ risk between 0.15% and 0.55% based on history and current test results (e.g., HPV-positive ASC-US or LSIL followed by a colposcopy result of <CIN 2, followed by a negative follow-up HPV test or cotest), perform repeat testing in 3 years with HPV-based testing. Estimated 5-year CIN 3+ risk at or above 0.55% based on history and current test results but below the threshold for immediate colposcopy of 4.0% (e.g., HPV-positive/NILM or HPV-negative/LSIL with unknown previous screening or colposcopy with biopsies of histologic LSIL [CIN 1]), perform repeat testing in 1 year with HPV-based testing. Estimated 5-year CIN 3+ risk at 4.0% or greater based on history and current test results (e.g., HPV-positive with ASC-US or LSIL cytology), refer for colposcopy. Estimated immediate risk of CIN 3+ of 60% or greater and nonpregnant, referral for excisional procedure without previous biopsy confirmation is preferred but colposcopy with biopsy is acceptable.

In women with an abnormal Pap smear requiring colposcopy follow-up, a normal colposcopy result is associated with a very low risk for squamous intraepithelial lesions; colposcopy in this setting has a sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 48% for distinguishing normal from abnormal cervices.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 studies, including 4 diagnostic cohort studies and 3 randomized clinical trials of patients with suspected cervical neoplasia, found no difference between endocervical brush and endocervical curettage in diagnostic accuracy for cervical cancer, inadequate sampling rate, or adverse effects, based on low-quality evidence.

Dynamic spectral imaging colposcopy (produces a digital interpretation and color-coded map of the colposcopic image following application of acetic acid) compared with conventional colposcopy may have higher sensitivity in detecting cervical lesions (79% vs. 55%, respectively, in one study).

Images obtained from use of a portable pocket colposcope, as part of an effort to improve telemedicine, were comparable to standard colposcopy with readings in agreement 83.1% of the time; adding Lugol's iodine as a secondary contrast agent improved the percent agreement.
Consider playing music during colposcopy to reduce anxiety and perceived pain. Use of video colposcopy does not reduce anxiety in women undergoing colposcopy.

Use of a small amount of lubricating gel on the speculum can reduce pain associated with the exam, even with a plastic speculum. Consider use of water-soluble lubricants not containing carbomers, especially if using liquid-based tests.
Consider endometrial cancer when foamy histiocytes (FH), FH plus benign endometrial cells or atypical endometrial cells are seen in cervicovaginal smears from postmenopausal women.
Folate receptor-mediated staining solution detection appears to have comparable sensitivity and higher specificity for detecting cervical cancer compared to HPV testing and cytology.

Acetic acid/Lugol's iodine staining: In a cross sectional study in India, visual inspection with acetic acid was more sensitive than cytology in detecting CIN2 or CIN3 lesions on biopsy among women >40 years of age (13.3% vs. 4.1%, respectively); for younger women, the two screening strategies were equivalent.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 3 cluster RCTs in India and one quasi-experimental study in Thailand concluded that use of visual inspection with acetic acid staining reduced both cervical cancer-specific mortality (pooled rate ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.56-0.81) and all-cause mortality (pooled rate ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.85-0.97) after a range of 7-12 years of follow-up.

In a Chinese study of screening with visual inspection with acetic acid/Lugol’s iodine in over 10,000 rural women, 0.85% (87/10,269) of women was diagnosed via pathology-confirmed biopsy with CIN1, 0.25% with CIN2, 0.27% with CIN3, and 0.02% (2/10,269) with cervical cancer. Follow-up screening at 1 year identified additional cases of CIN2 and CIN3, but no additional cases of cervical cancer.

Use of visual inspection with Lugol's iodine was found to be more sensitive than visual inspection with acetic acid in a meta-analysis of 15 studies in sub-Saharan Africa; pooled sensitivity and specificity were similar for HPV testing compared with either of the two visual methods, and prevalence of CIN2+ did not vary by screening test.

Use of cytologic immunostaining with p16 and Ki67 antibodies using liquid cytology samples or biopsy specimens appears to improve test characteristics of Pap smears and identify more women with higher grade lesions.

In a Chinese study, p16(INK4A) staining of CIN1 biopsy specimens at baseline was associated with an increased risk of finding high-grade CIN over 2 years of follow-up (OR 1.43; 95% CI, 0.52-3.91). In another study, application of CellDetect® staining technique to conventional slides and Thinprep smears of 600 patients had a sensitivity of 94.34% and specificity of 88.73% for detecting CIN or squamous cell carcinoma.
In a population of HPV-positive women in Norway, p16/Ki-67 dual staining was more sensitive (0.88 vs. 0.79) but less specific (0.28 vs. 0.35) than cytology for predicting high-grade CIN.

HPV DNA integration into the host genome leads to high-level expression of the viral oncogenes, E6 and E7, which cause cell transformation and potentially cervical cancer. HPV integration is considered a necessary event in the progression to cervical cancer and the number of integration sites is associated with cervical cancer and precancer. For example, the frequency of HPV integration for high-risk HPV genotypes is consistently high.

Using tissue specimens, several methods can be used to study HPV integration sites. These include amplification of papillomavirus oncogene transcripts, detection of integrated papillomavirus sequences by ligation-mediated PCR, and next-generation sequencing (also referred to as high-throughput viral integration detection [HIVID] which enables parallel sequencing of a large number of nucleic acid molecules simultaneously).

In an observational study including 1392 patients aged 25 to 65 years with no prior history of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher, HPV integration testing was compared to cytology triage within 3 months after a positive primary HPV testing result. The presence of at least 5 sequences of viral DNA was considered a positive result and was verified by PCR testing. Histology was the gold standard for final diagnosis. Patients with HPV 16 and positive HPV integration had similar sensitivity of 71%, but higher specificity (95% vs. 64%) than cytology triage. Using a strategy of HPV integration testing to triage patients with a positive HPV test might reduce colposcopy referral; however, costs of this stratgey are unknown.

Detection of circulating cell-free HPV DNA appears to be a useful biomarker for cervical cancer. Authors of a meta-analysis of 15 studies including 684 patients with cervical cancer found a pooled positive likelihood ratio of 6.85 (95% CI 3.09-15.21), negative likelihood ratio of 0.60 (95% CI 0.46-0.78), diagnostic odds ratio of 15.25 (95% CI 5.42-42.94), and area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.94 (95% CI 0.89-0.99). The diagnostic role for oncogenic circulating RNAs was similar with an AUC of 0.93 for cervical cancer.

Additional biomarkers are under investigation and several have been identified that predict severity of HPV-associated cervical disease. Methylated human gene biomarkers show promise for detecting CIN2/3 from cytology specimens.

In a study of 145 women, elevated methylation level was associated with increased disease severity (CIN3, 17.9% [±7.2] vs. CIN2, 11.6% [±6.5] or vs. CIN1, 9.0% [±3.5]). Using a methylation threshold of 14.0%, overall accuracy of predicting CIN3 was 76.7%.
Use of a scoring system for CIN1-3 based on immunohistochemical biomarkers Ki-67 and p16ink4a improved accuracy and reproducibility of cytology grading of cervical specimens in one study.

For pretreatment planning of invasive cervical cancer, the American College of Radiology and International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) recommend magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pelvis without and with IV contrast and fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography-computed tomography (FDG-PET/CT) whole body as appropriate for staging.

Authors of a meta-analysis of imaging modalities for determining extent of disease based on 115 studies with 13,999 patients with newly-diagnosed cervical cancer concluded that MRI was the method of choice for assessing local extent, with ultrasound of value if MRI was unavailable. CT, MRI, or PET were useful for detection of lymph node metastases based on all three having high specificity (0.88-0.98) although with low sensitivity (0.29-0.69).

With respect to diagnosis of cervical cancer lymph node metastasis, authors of a meta-analysis of 11 studies found a similar sensitivity (0.65 and 0.58) and specificity (0.93 and 0.91) for PET-CT and MRI, respectively, but a significantly higher AUC for PET-CT (0.824 vs. 0.702 for MRI); the latter finding may be influenced by study design and use of blinding methods. Other authors found MRI accurate for evaluating the distance between the tumor and the internal os, stromal infiltration, and parametrial invasion, but less accurate for diagnosing lymph node metastases.

Ultrasound and MRI were found to have similar diagnostic performance for detecting parametrial infiltration in women with cervical cancer based on a meta-analysis of 9 studies. However, authors of a meta-analysis of 11 studies found limited usefulness of ultrasound as a diagnostic tool for local staging of cervical cancer, based on pooled sensitivity and specificity of TVUS for parametrial invasion of 62% (95% CI 40-80) and 91% (95% CI 79-97), for stromal invasion of 84% (95% CI 77-90) and 80% (95% CI 61-91), and for lymph node metastasis of 52% (95% CI 8-93) and 95% (95% CI 68-99). There was significant study heterogeneity.

Imaging appears comparable to surgical nodal assessment with respect to progression-free survival (hazard ratio [HR] 1.13, 95% CI 0.73-1.74) and overall survival (HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.66-1.69) based on a systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 studies with 1112 patients.
Individualized screening guidelines can be accessed using an online calculator available at the USPSTF Web site (http://www.ahrq.gov/clinic/uspstfix.htm).

Shared-decision making allows women to have an active role in treatment decisions. In an Australian study including 1638 women who were presented with a hypothetical diagnosis of CIN2 and provided information on the benefits and harms of different management options, most women (79%) chose active surveillance over surgery.

Follow-up recommendations for abnormal PAP smears and/or positive HPV testing are available from ACOG. Options for treatment of CIN are observation or excision (hysterectomy, cold-knife cone biopsy, loop electrosurgical excision procedure [LEEP]) or ablation (cryotherapy, thermal coagulation) of the cervical transformation zone. Excisional techniques reduce the risk of treatment failure, A but increase the risk of subsequent preterm birth. B

National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) 2023 guidelines provide guidance regarding treatment of invasive cervical cancer by stage. B In this update, the clinical staging and primary treatment recommendations were extensively revised to include conservative surgery criteria recommendations based on the published ConCerv Trial data.
For early cervical cancer, abdominal radical hysterectomy is associated with improved overall and disease-free survival compared to minimally-invasive procedures. A
Among those with locally-advanced cervical cancer, chemoradiation with or without hysterectomy appears to have the best results for survival. B

For patients with more advanced disease, local treatment (resection, local ablative therapies) should be considered if the disease is believed amenable to local therapy or systemic and supportive therapy offered. C Monoclonal antibody therapy (i.e., bevacizumab or cemiplimab) can be considered based on limited supporting evidence. B

The prevalence of female sexual dysfunction, urinary incontinence, and fecal incontinence in cervical cancer survivors after treatment was 45.0% (95% CI, 21.8-68.3%), 34.1% (95% CI, 25.5-42.7%), and 11.1% (95% CI, 4.8-17.3%) based on a meta-analysis of 14 studies. There was high study heterogeneity.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs and 2 retrospective cohort studies of survivors of treatment for cervical cancer found that pelvic floor muscle training with counseling and yoga or core exercises were beneficial for sexual function (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.96, 95% CI -1.22 to -0.70) and health-related quality of life (SMD 0.63, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.88).

Pelvic insufficiency fractures can occur following radiation treatment for cervical cancer. Authors of a meta-analysis of 15 studies with 3633 patients found a pooled prevalence of 14% (95% CI 10-19%) with a higher incidence reported in studies that used MRI as a diagnostic tool (17%, 95% CI 12-22%).

Vaginal stenosis also occurs following radiation treatment. In an RCT with 195 women, all patients had a mean reduction in vaginal volume of 25.47%, but use of a vaginal dilator compared to estrogen or testosterone treatment resulted in a lower frequency and severity of vaginal stenosis at 1 year.

Options for treatment of CIN are observation or excision (hysterectomy, cold-knife cone biopsy, loop electrosurgical excision procedure [LEEP]) or ablation (cryotherapy, thermal coagulation) of the cervical transformation zone.
Women with ASC-US cytology and negative HPV test results, should undergo dual testing (co-testing) in 3 years.

Women aged 30 years and older who are cytology-negative but HPV-positive should either: 1) repeat dual testing in 12 months; if negative, repeat testing in 3 years and if worsening cytology or continued HPV refer for colposcopy or 2) undergo immediate HPV genotype-specific testing for HPV-16 and HPV-18; if negative conduct dual testing in 12 months and if positive refer for colposcopy.

In one study of 195 women who were persistently HPV positive, all 40 women who continued recommended follow-up and demonstrated HPV persistence and 15/21 women with unknown persistence developed CIN2 or worse, most within 6 years.

HPV genotype-specific testing is supported by results of 10-year follow up of the ARTISTIC trial in which 24,496 women attending routine cervical screening in Greater Manchester were randomly allocated in a ratio of 3:1 to have their HPV result revealed and acted upon or concealed. CIN3 risk was largely confined to those with persistent high-risk HPV types with a 10-year cumulative risk of CIN3+ of 19.4%; 95% CI, 15.8%-23.8% for women with HPV16/18 infection and borderline/low-grade cytology and 10.7%, 95% CI, 8.3%-13.9% for those with HPV16/18 infection and normal cytology compared to women with other HPV types (7.3%, 95% CI, 5.4%-9.7% with borderline/low-grade cytology and 3.2%, 95% CI, 2.2%-4.5% with normal cytology).

Based on a large Swedish cohort study, among women aged 22 to 27 years with cytology showing abnormal squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASCUS) or low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL), the incidence of invasive cervical cancer did not differ for those undergoing repeat cytology within 6 months or colposcopy with biopsy within 6 months.

Women with abnormal cytology are at risk of progression. In the Swedish population study noted above, women screened with abnormal results in their 50s had average cumulative incidences of cervical cancer up to age 80 years of 9.7/1000 with low-grade lesions and 15.3/1000 with high-grade lesions if screening was not continued; this rate is compared to 1.6/1000 for those with adequate screening in their 50s and normal results.

However, there is a high rate of regression of CIN2 without treatment. In a study of 98 young women and adolescents, regression occurred in 68% by 3 years and in a retrospective cohort study of 157 women with CIN2 or CIN2/3 whose health care providers offered conservative management, 98 (62%) showed spontaneous regression at a median of 8 months follow-up.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies with a range of about 1200-1400 non-pregnant women with CIN2 found rates of regression at 24 months of 50% (95% CI, 43%-57%); persistence rate was 32% (95% CI, 23%-42%) and progression was found in 18% (11%-27%). As above, regression rates were highest in women <30 years at 60% with 11% having disease progression.

In a Swedish cohort study of 137 women with CIN2 to establish the natural history of disease, CIN2 regressed partially or totally in 68 of 82 (83%) patients with HPV status other than HPV 16, but only in 23 of 45 (51%) patients with HPV 16, making watchful waiting a reasonable option, particularly for women without HPV 16. Only 1 patient with HPV 16 had progression to stage 1A1 cervical cancer during the study period.
Procedures for CIN

In a single-center RCT of 400 African women with HIV infection and CIN grade 2 or 3 randomized to cryotherapy or LEEP, rates of recurrent CIN2-3 were higher at 2 years for women in the cryotherapy group (30% vs. 19%, relative risk 1.71; 95% CI, 1.12-2.65). Adverse event rates were similar and occurred in 40 women (45 events) in the cryotherapy group and in 30 women (38 events) in the LEEP group.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 studies comparing procedural treatment for CIN found that treatment with cold knife decreased risk of residual disease compared with LEEP (RR 0.54, 95%CI 0.30-0.96). Cryotherapy, compared with LEEP, increased risk of disease recurrence (RR 1.86, 95%CI 1.16-2.97, p = 0.01) and increased risk of infections (RR 1.17, 95%CI 1.08-1.28), but decreased risk of minor bleeding (RR 0.49, 95%CI 0.40-0.59).

In a systematic review of 6 studies comparing head-to-head ablative and excisional techniques to treat CIN2/3, excisional treatment was more effective with respect to recurrence at 6, 12, and 24 months (RR at 24 months comparing ablative to excisional treatment was 1.57, 95% CI 1.11-2.23). Both procedures had similar safety profiles.

However, ablative treatments probably do not increase risk of preterm birth. Authors of a meta-analysis found increased risk of preterm birth for all excisional techniques compared to the untreated colposcopy group (cold-knife conization: 2.27 [1.70-3.02]; laser conization: 1.77 [1.29-2.43]; and large loop excision of the transformation zone: 1.37 [1.16-1.62]). No differences were found for ablative methods including laser ablation, cryotherapy, and cold coagulation. Most evidence was based on observational studies.

In a prospective study of 216 women with HSIL and treated with loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP), intraoperative HPV testing using the Hybrid Capture 2 system was highly predictive of HSIL recurrence, which occurred in 6%, with sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative predictive values of 85.7%, 80.8%, 24.0% and 98.8%, respectively, compared to HPV testing at 6 months (76.9%, 75.8%, 17.2% and 98.0%, respectively).

HPV genotyping following treatment for high-grade CIN appears to be more useful for discriminated risk of posttreatment high-grade CIN than qualitative HPV based on a systematic review of seven studies deemed to be at low risk of bias. While sensitivity for both preoperative testing methods approached 100%, positive predictive value (PPV) was higher when the same genotype was identified pre and post-treatment than with qualitative testing (median PPV 44% vs. 22%, respectively)

Surgery is often used to treat CIN and is associated with blood loss. Authors of a Cochrane review found that use of vasopressin significantly reduced perioperative bleeding compared to placebo and tranexamic acid reduces secondary hemorrhage after knife and laser cone biopsy. In addition, Packing with Monsel's solution also reduced perioperative blood loss and decreased risk of dysmenorrhoea (RR 0.37; 95% CI, 0.16-0.84) and cervical stenosis (RR 0.35; 95% CI, 0.25-0.49) compared to routine suturing.

Photodynamic therapy (light and a photosensitizing chemical substance used in conjunction with molecular oxygen to elicit cancer cell death) may be useful in increasing complete remission rates among those with CIN (OR 2.51; 95% CI, 1.23-5.12) and HPV infection (OR 3.82; 95% CI, 1.91-7.65) based on a meta-analysis of 4 low-quality RCTs.

Use of SAM vaginal gel, a medical device containing adsorptive silicon dioxide and antioxidative sodium selenite and citric acid, for three 28-day periods in women with CIN2 or p16-possitive CIN1 resulted in a greater number of patients experiencing regression of CIN lesions compared to the control group (78/108 patients [72.2%] and 27/108 patients [25%], respectively) at 3 months.
Pre-procedural oral mefenamic acid before LEEP procedure with intracervical lidocaine injection was not associated with pain reduction.

NCCN guidelines (2023) provide guidance regarding treatment of disease by FIGO 2018 staging system. A discussion update, however, is in progress.. Recommended workup for women with cervical cancer includes a complete blood count with platelets, liver and renal function, and consideration of HIV testing. Chest X-ray should be considered, followed by chest computed tomography (CT) without contrast if an abnormality is found. Other recommended tests based on stage include pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)/CT.

Treatment for Stage IA1 disease is divided into fertility sparing and non-fertility sparing approaches and begins with cone biopsy. In cases with no lymphovascular space invasion, options include cone biopsy alone or with pelvic lymphadenectomy or sentinel lymph node mapping.

The ConCerv trial was a prospective, single-arm, 16-site multicenter study to evaluate conservative surgery in 100 participants who met the following criteria: 1) FIGO 2009 stage IA2-IB1 cervical carcinoma; 2) squamous cell (any grade) or adenocarcinoma (grade 1 or 2 only) histology; 3) tumor size <2 cm; 4) no lymphovascular space invasion; 5) depth of invasion <10 mm; 6) negative imaging for metastatic disease; and 7) negative conization margins. Surgery included conization followed by lymph node assessment in 44 women, conization followed by simple hysterectomy with lymph node assessment in 40 women, and inadvertent (invasive cancer diagnosed postoperatively) simple hysterectomy followed by lymph node dissection in 16 women. Positive lymph nodes were noted in 5 patients (5%). Residual disease in the post-conization hysterectomy specimen was noted in 1/40 patients; an immediate failure rate of 2.5%. At a median follow-up of 36.3 months (range 0.0-68.3), three patients developed recurrent disease within 2 years of surgery, one who underwent conization alone, none in the conization followed by simple hysterectomy group and 2 in the inadvertent simple hysterectomy group.

listitem.strong: Open radical hysterectomy vs. minimally-invasive surgery

list.listitem: In an epidemiologic study, survival for women with early (stage IA2 or IB1) cervical cancer following radical hysterectomy was higher using open surgery compared to minimally invasive surgery, with mortality rates of 5.3% vs. 9.1%, respectively at Commission on Cancer-accredited hospitals in the United States. This finding was supported by an RCT of 631 women with primarily stage IB1 cervical cancer, in which women randomized to open abdominal radical hysterectomy compared to minimally invasive surgery had higher 3-year rates of disease-free survival (97.1% vs. 91.2%, respectively) and overall survival (99% vs. 93.8%).

In an RCT of 536/631 women with stage IA1 with lymph-vascular invasion to IB1 cervical cancer randomized to minimally-invasive surgery or open radical hysterectomy, the trial was suspended early due to an increased risk of recurrence and death in the minimally invasive surgery group. Rates of intraoperative and postoperative complications were similar.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs comparing types of surgery for patients with early-stage cervical cancer found overall survival improved with open hysterectomy compared to laparoscopic hysterectomy (RR 0.97, 95%CI 0.96-0.98). Of the laparoscopic procedures, a technique using no uterine manipulator in combination with vaginal colpotomy had the best results for overall and disease-free survival.

This finding was confirmed in a meta-analysis of 22 studies with 14,894 patients that demonstrated decreased overall (hazard ratio [HR] 1.23, 95%CI 1.03-1.43) and disease-free survival (HR 1.25, 95% CI 1.07-1.42) for patients undergoing minimally-invasive surgery compared to abdominal radical hysterectomy. In another meta-analysis, the pooled hazard of recurrence or death was 71% higher among patients who underwent minimally invasive radical hysterectomy compared with those who underwent open surgery.

While authors of a meta-analysis of 14 studies did not find a difference in overall survival for minimally-invasive surgery vs abdominal hysterectomy, the odds of progression-free survival were worse for women undergoing minimally-invasive radical hysterectomy and progressively worse with increased longer follow-up (HR 1.48 for >36 months, HR 1.69 for >48 months, and HR 2.02 for >60 months).

In another meta-analysis of 27 studies comparing the two procedures, minimally-invasive surgery (laparoscopic or robotic-assisted) was associated with higher risk of intraoperative overall complications (OR 1.41, 95%CI 1.07-1.86) but significantly lower risk of postoperative aggregate complications (i.e. complications of transfusion, wound infection, pelvic infection and abscess, lymphedema, intestinal obstruction, pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, and urinary tract infection; OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.34-0.48).

However, authors of a secondary analysis of an RCT including 631 patients randomized to minimally-invasive surgery vs. open surgery, at a median follow-up of 3 years with approximately 78% of enrolled patients, there were no differences in quality of life measured by the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Cervical score.

Some of the differences reported in favor of abdominal surgery over minimally-invasive surgery may be due to publication characteristics, center-geography and sample volume. There do not appear to be differences between procedures for patients with stage IB1 cervical cancer.

In a case series of 116 patients with cervical cancer stages IB-IIA who underwent total mesometrial resection (en bloc resection of the uterus, proximal vagina, and mesometrium [majority of the broad ligament of the uterus]) and therapeutic lymphadenectomy without chemoradiation, 25.0% of whom were lymph node-positive, overall recurrence rate was 7.8% in a median follow-up of 24 months. Locoregional recurrences occurred in 6.0% and. one patient died from the disease during the observation period.

The American Society for Radiation Oncology (2020) recommend chemoradiation for stages IB3-IVA. Radiation therapy or chemoradiation is conditionally recommended for stages IA1-IB2 if medically inoperable. Brachytherapy is strongly recommended for all patients receiving definitive radiation therapy.

Preoperative neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by radical surgery was comparable to radical surgery alone for women with FIGO Stage I-II cervical cancer with respect to overall and progression-free survival based on a meta-analysis of 16 studies.

For women with stage IB2-IIA cervical cancer, authors of a meta-analysis of 7 studies with 687 patients found improved overall survival with radical hysterectomy compared with those of chemoradiotherapy (HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.36-0.67).

In an RCT of 147 women with Stage IIIB cervical cancer, those randomized to chemoradiotherapy had better disease-free survival but not improved overall survival compared to radiotherapy alone. However, in a follow-up study of up to 14 years for 146 women from the original cohort, chemoradiotherapy improved both disease-free and overall survival.

Authors of a meta-analysis of RCTs found concurrent chemoradiotherapy more effective than neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by radical hysterectomy for overall survival among those with locally-advanced cervical cancer (HR 1.25, 95%CI 1.02-1.54).

Based on a systematic review of 14 studies including 2302 patients, there was little survival benefit of adding hysterectomy to chemoradiotherapy among women with locally-advanced cervical cancer, and hysterectomy was accompanied by considerable perioperative morbidity.

Similarly, in a meta-analysis of 3 RCTs and 2 case-control studies of women with stage IB2, IIA, or IIB cervical cancer, there was no difference in overall survival or disease-free survival comparing neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by radical surgery (NACT+RS) with radiotherapy only or concurrent chemoradiotherapy. However, for the population with median follow-up over 60 months, a subgroup analysis did demonstrate a benefit of NACT+RS for both overall and disease-free survival (HR 0.431, 95%CI 0.238-0.781 and HR 0.300, 95%CI 0.187-0.482, respectively) but at a cost of a higher incidence of thrombocytopenia (RR 3.240, 95% CI 1.575-6.662).

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 studies – 2 RCTs, one matched-case study, and the remainder small retrospective cohort studies (including a total of 2150 patients - found no clear benefit of adjunctive chemotherapy after chemoradiation for overall survival or progression-free survival for patients with locally advanced cervical cancer.

For patients with 1A1 to 1A2 disease with lymphovascular space invasion, the NCCN 2023 guideline recommends modified radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy and consideration of sentinel lymph node mapping OR pelvic external beam radiotherapy and brachytherapy for patients who are medically inoperable or refuse surgery.

In a Chinese RCT, 1048 women treated with radical hysterectomy for stage IB to IIA cervical cancer with adverse pathological factors were randomized to postoperative adjunctive therapy with sequential chemoradiation, concurrent chemoradiation or radiation therapy alone. Sequential chemoradiation was the most effective and resulted in higher disease-free survival and lower risk of cancer death (5-year rate, 92.0% vs 88.0%; HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.35-0.95 after adjustment for lymph node involvement) compared to radiation alone; the latter performed similarly to concurrent chemoradiation.

For patients with early-stage cervical cancer, defined as FIGO 2018 stages IA-IB1-IB2-IIA1, it is unclear if adding adjunctive treatment with radiotherapy is of benefit following radical hysterectomy when lymph nodes are negative. Authors of a systematic review including 2 RCTs, 2 prospective and 4 retrospective cohort studies found no difference in recurrence or mortality risk for the 842 participants who underwent radical hysterectomy alone compared to the 554 who underwent surgery plus radiotherapy.

Adjunctive brachytherapy following chemoradiation may be an effective option for women with locoregional disease. Based on a disease registry of 1416 patients with stage IB-IVA disease or stage IVB disease restricted to paraaortic lymph metastasis, this combination of treatment resulted in 5-year local control of 92% (95% CI 90-93). With respect to adverse effects, actuarial cumulative 5-year incidence of grade 3-5 morbidity was 8.5% (6.9-10.6) for gastrointestinal events, 6.8% (95% CI 5.4-8.6) for genitourinary events, 5.7% (4.3-7.6) for vaginal events, and 3.2% (2.2-4.5) for fistulae.

Preoperative brachytherapy for patients with early-stage cervical cancer was found to improve 5-year survival compared with the up-front surgery (OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.11-2.84, I2 = 0%), based on 10 non-randomized trials and improved recurrence rates in 3 RCTs (OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.13-0.91, I2 not applicable) but not in the non-randomized trials.

Authors of a systematic review found insufficient evidence from RCTs to determine whether hysterectomy with radiotherapy, with or without chemotherapy, improves survival for women with locally-advanced cervical cancer who were treated with radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy alone.

NCCN guidelines (2023) recommend that for stage IVB disease or in patients with distant metastases, local treatment (resection, local ablative therapies) should be considered if the disease is felt to be amenable to local therapy. Adjuvant systemic therapy can also be considered.

Depending on surgical findings (e.g., positive margins, positive lymph nodes), NCCN 2023 guideline recommendations for adjunctive treatment may include pelvic external beam radiotherapy, concurrent platinum-containing chemotherapy, or vaginal brachytherapy. Alternative chemotherapy regimens are provided

Anti-angiogenesis agents are under investigation as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy in persistent, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer. Authors of a review of these studies found low-certainty evidence supporting use of bevacizumab plus chemotherapy on survival but with an increase in specific adverse events (gastrointestinal perforations or fistulae, thromboembolic events, hypertension) and serious adverse events. They found no support for use of cediranib plus chemotherapy, apatinib plus chemotherapy, apatinib plus chemotherapy/brachytherapy, or pazopanib monotherapy and there was evidence of worse outcomes with pazopanib plus lapatinib.

In an RCT of 227 patients with advanced cervical cancer receiving chemotherapy with bevacizumab, 148 (65%) discontinued study protocol treatment, 90 for disease progression and 58 for toxicity. Median survival time from treatment discontinuation to death for these 2 groups of patients was 7.9 months and 12.1 months, respectively. Patients who discontinued chemotherapy with bevacizumab for toxicity, however, had a significantly greater decline in quality of life than those with progression.

In an RCT including 617 patients with persistent, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer, addition of the monoclonal antibody pembrolizumab vs. placebo to platinum-based chemotherapy with or without bevacizumab resulted in increased progression-free survival by several months (10.4 months vs. 8.2 months, HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.79) and improved overall survival at 24 months (53.0% vs. 41.7%, HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.81).

Cemiplimab, a PD-1 blocking antibody, administered every 3 weeks was more effective than single-agent chemotherapy for women with recurrent cervical cancer after first-line platinum-containing chemotherapy resulting in significantly longer overall survival (12.0 months vs. 8.5 months; HR for death 0.69, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.84). Similar rates of grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred (45% with cemiplimab and 53.4% with chemotherapy).

A trial randomized 502 persons with recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer to tisotumab vedotin or investigator's choice of alternate chemotherapy (topotecan, irinotecan, gemcitabine, or vinorelbine). Overall survival was slightly longer with tisotumab (11.5 vs 9.5 months, p = 0.004).

Among 36 women with histologically-confirmed recurrent or advanced HPV-positive (HPV-16 or HPV-18) cervical cancer, combination GX-188E therapeutic DNA vaccine plus pembrolizumab resulted in an overall response in 11 women at 24 weeks with four (15%) having a complete response and seven (27%) a partial response. Sixteen (44%) had treatment-related adverse events with four (11%) having grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events.
For women with metastatic disease not amenable to local therapy, systemic therapy or supportive care are recommended.

Based on data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology and End-Results (SEER) Program, 5-year relative survival from cervical cancer is 67.2% (2013-2019). Five-year survival for those with localized disease is 91.2%, regional disease 59.8%, and for those with distant metastases 18.9%. The age-adjusted death rates have been falling about 0.8% each year from 2010 to 2019.

The five-year survival rate for HPV-associated cervical cancer was 64.2% based on data from 27 population-based cancer registries covering approximately 59% of the US population; relative survival was higher for white compared to black patients. The most recent estimate for 5-year survival from the CDC is 66.1%.

Predictors of survival for patients with cervical cancer based on a meta-analysis of 140 studies with 47,965 patients were age; cell type; depth of tumor invasion; FIGO stage; hemoglobin level; histological grade; leukocytosis; lymph node involvement; lymph-vascular space invasion; neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio; parametrial invasion; platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio; resection margin; squamous cell carcinoma antigen level; thrombocytosis; and tumor grade, size, and volume.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 89 studies of patients with CIN found that most cases of CIN1 or CIN2 (60%, 95% CI 55-65% for CIN1 and 55%, 95% CI 50-60% for CIN2) regress spontaneously in less than 24 months; the highest rates of regression are among young women and those who are hrHPV-negative. Progression to cancer for CIN1/2 was less than 0.5%. Among those with CIN3, regression occurred in 28% (95% CI 17-41%) with 67% having persistent disease (95% CI 36-91%), and 2% progressing (95% CI 0-25%).

In a meta-analysis of 10 studies of pregnant women with high-grade CIN, regression, persistence and progression rates were 40% (95% CI 35-45%), 59% (95% CI 54-64%) and 1% (95% CI 0-2%), respectively. There was moderate heterogeneity between studies.

Among patients treated with cold knife conization or a loop electrosurgical excision of CIN2+, persistence of HPV 16 genotype was significantly correlated with recurrent high-grade disease and persistent infection after treatment.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 studies with 1663 patients who underwent radical hysterectomy for IB1 cervical cancer found an incidence rate of relapse of 10.6%. There were no differences observed in relapse rate based on type of surgery (open vs. laparoscopic).

Early non-response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy was significantly associated with higher recurrence of cervical cancer in a meta-analysis of 9 studies including 1,462 responders and 490 non-responders. The hazard ratios for disease-free survival at 1, 3, and 5 years among responders was 0.25 (95% CI: 0.14-0.43), 0.26 (95% CI: 0.16-0.43), and 0.26 (95% CI: 0.16-0.42) using RECIST criteria.

HPV testing may be helpful for detecting recurrence following radiotherapy. Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 cohort studies with 1,055 patients with cervical cancer who had received pelvic radiation with or without chemotherapy found an overall pooled sensitivity and specificity of HPV DNA testing of 0.84 (95% CI 0.66-0.94) and 0.35 (95% CI 0.20-0.54), respectively. The positive and negative likelihood ratios were 1.3 (95% CI=1.0-1.7) and 0.45 (95% CI=0.18-1.10), respectively.

feature.caption: Terminology of Pap Smear Report Based on 2001 Bethesda System.
feature.feature_body:
Term Distinguishing Features Management
ASCUS (atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance) Squamous cell abnormalities not fulfilling strict criteria for dysplasia; most common abnormality screened Repeat Pap smear, HPV testing, and colposcopy are possible management strategies
ASCH (atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL) As above except HSIL may be part of the sample Colposcopy
LSIL (low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion) Cellular changes favoring HPV involvement, mild dysplasia, or CIN 1 Colposcopy with biopsy; excisional and ablative procedures in initial management not performed without confirmed CIN
HSIL (high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion) Cellular changes favoring moderate and severe dysplasia, CIN 2 or CIN 3, or carcinoma in situ Colposcopy with endocervical sampling; immediate excision likely appropriate for visible lesions in select populations
Atypical glandular cells Endocervical or endometrial seen Colposcopy with endocervical sampling and endometrial sampling
Data from Solomon D, Davey D, Kurman R, Forum Group Members Bethesda 2001 Workshop. The 2001 Bethesda System: terminology for reporting results of cervical cytology. JAMA 2002;287:2114–2119. Wright TC, Jr., Cox JT, Massad LS, Twiggs LB, Wilkinson EJ, ASCCP-Sponsored Consensus Conference. 2001 consensus guidelines for the management of women with cervical cytological abnormalities. JAMA 2002;287:2120–2129.
